Pitfalls of “Adversarial” Reviews

Adversarial reviews are often touted as the panacea for all agentic ills, but in my experience, they’re a much weaker safeguard than made out to be, and can fail in predictable ways.

A fundamental problem with adversarial reviews is that they cannot in any way vouch for the completeness of the factual tier. At best, an adversarial reviewer can verify whether a hypothesis satisfies the constraints already in the factual tier. It cannot know when a constraint is absent, so it cannot detect the “too few constraints” problem.

Another problem with adversarial reviews is they run the risk of confirming the main agent’s priors, if the adversarial reviewer uses the same model, has the same context, looks at the same code, pores over the telemetry data, and so forth as the main agent. In such cases, two agents concurring can be seen as one opinion counted twice.

This isn’t to suggest adversarial reviews are entirely pointless. Only that an adversarial review cannot be trusted to work as instrument of verification. It works better as an instrument of elimination, when it tries to contradict, rather than corroborate a hypothesis.

Contradiction is a stronger and easier test because of how the framework operates. A hypothesis is only valid if it satisfies every fact. No number of confirmations can prove a hypothesis, because there there’s always a possibility that there’s some crucial fact missing in the factual tier that an adversarial reviewer is unaware of (the “unknown unknowns”). In the case of the “latency bug”, one of my initial instructions to Claude was to have an independent subagent validate any theories it came up with. The cert reloading theory survived an independent subagent’s validation. The subagent had no way to disprove it, because the fact that disproved it (a trace showing the certificate being loaded only once) hadn’t been gathered yet. Once that fact was available to the factual tier, the hypothesis was invalidated immediately.

How to Incorporate an Adversarial Review Into The Three Step Debugging Loop

Adversarial reviews should be incorporated into every step of the debugging process described above. At every step, the adversarial reviewer’s core objective is the same: try to eliminate something rather than prove its validity.

Step 1: Isolate high-fidelity signals in the factual tier

The adversarial reviewer should first check if the high-fidelity signals also show up in the control. Those that do are noise. They can’t steer the agent.

Next, the adversarial reviewer should check if the control isn’t broken in the same way as the variable, because a control with the same bug turns every real signal into noise.

Finally, the adversarial reviewer should also check how each fact was gathered. A fact gathered from the wrong host, during the wrong time window, or with the wrong version of a tool can make the right hypothesis look incorrect.

Step 2: Isolate the most promising hypothesis in the derivative tier

Firstly, the adversarial reviewer should estimate how many hypotheses satisfy each signal, without pursuing any of them. A signal that almost any hypothesis can satisfy isn’t a strong one, and any hypothesis derived from it is very unlikely to be the root cause.

Secondly, the adversarial reviewer should read the “hypotheses-by-facts” matrix row by row. If none of the hypotheses satisfy all the facts, the adversarial reviewer should verify that the agent tried using tactics 2 to 4 to either merge, split, or combine existing hypotheses into forms that’d make them more amenable to steering the agent before formulating an entirely new hypothesis.

Finally, the adversarial reviewer should check that the agent only descends a layer when every signal is weak, or when every hypothesis still falls short even after applying “the five tactics”.

![Integrating an adversarial reviewer into the 3 step debugging process](/items/itm_c8a47bce/images/2fec37bc7c37ff58788165369eb099684226a14c87e4dce2572fd4feef4e773a)

Step 3: Validate the most promising hypothesis against every constraint in the factual tier

A hypothesis is only valid if it satisfies every fact, so it’s enough for an adversarial reviewer to find a single fact that’s not satisfied by the hypothesis. Requiring citations is a practical way to achieve this. Citations require an agent to fish out evidence from the factual tier. When I was debugging “the hang”, about a third of the claims I challenged could not be backed up by citations and were culled forthwith.

In the case of a combined hypothesis, a contradicting fact should be enough to immediately spell out which individual hypothesis fails. The adversarial reviewer should also try removing each cause from the combined hypothesis to test whether all the causes are strictly necessary.

Retooling the Agentic Factory Floor For Autonomy And Accountability

The guiding principle when it comes to building “software factories” should be to have an agent-native debugging process in place where no human involvement will be necessary to diagnose and validate all types of bugs.

Mind The Gap

Every human intervention spells a gap in the process. All the three bugs chronicled in this post required manual intervention for the agent to get to the root cause. Each intervention brought something new to the table (a control, a constraint, a new check) that an agent ought to have procured itself.

That suggests that every human intervention is an opportunity for improvement, and a true agent-native software factory should treat it as such. The number of human interventions per bug is the most honest measure of how “agent-native” a factory really is, and the goal is for this number to be close to zero.

Agents Versus Humans: A Framework for Tradeoffs

Most existing debugging tools, processes, and frameworks were built for a human audience. We don’t default to emitting logs at trace level so as to not drown a human in noise, we aggregate telemetry into dashboards so as to make it easier for humans to interpret, we use visualizations like waterfall diagrams, bar charts, line graphs etc to aid with human interpretability.

A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent. The server-side P99 latency measurement in the “latency bug” was a perfect metric for a human audience. As a constraint for an agent, it was nearly useless, because almost any hypothesis could explain it.

When the two goals are at cross-purposes, a useful way to reconcile the tension is to:

  • optimize the factual tier for agents
  • optimize the decision points for humans
  • then turn those decision points into a future policy playbook

Agents require a “fat factual tier” to be scientific when it comes to root-causing bugs. It’s the job of the software factory to make sure every bit of data that’s possibly procurable is made available to the agent. This requires the software factory to have access to a large number of data sources: telemetry systems, production environments, source control systems, and ideally even (within reason) end-users’ desktops, devices etc. This poses serious security and privacy concerns, which can hamstring how truly autonomous a debugging agent can be. The software factory needs to devise a mechanism to get an agent graduated access to data sources which are read-only by default, scoped to the current investigation, time-limited, load and rate limit aware, privacy-scrubbed, and auditable.

“Optimizing the decision points for humans” doesn’t mean requiring a human to be responsible for every decision an agent makes. Our overarching goal is still to have minimal to no human involvement required in the diagnosis or validation of a bug. But acting on a diagnosis can involve decisions that carry political risk and accountability, and cannot be solely owned by an agent. Figuring out whether to roll back a new feature that’s slow but otherwise functional, whether to escalate a bug with a different team, whether to drop support for a specific feature, and so forth are examples of such decisions that need human involvement. Such decisions should be codified into future policy that an agent can apply.

Some decisions, however, can’t be made by an agent by simply applying a predetermined, broad brush policy. The “memory leak” had more than one potential fix (turn off the process-wide cache OR make the state machine safe to use inside the process-wide cache), each with different tradeoffs that required a human to decide how best to proceed. The agent’s job in such cases is to present all available choices to the human in an unambiguous way, along with its reasoning.

The Paradigm Shift In Thinking Required In The Agent-Native Vanguard

Becoming truly agent-native requires a few major shifts in thinking, and each of them inverts habits formed in the era when debugging was the sole preserve of humans.

Designing Verification > Understanding Code

Heretofore, a human’s value in the investigative process came from their mental model of the code. As I argued earlier, that mental model is slowly eroding. What ought to replace it isn’t a better mental model of the code (inasmuch as it isn’t going to be possible for engineers to build crystal clear mental models of frenetically changing code going forward) but a better methodology for reliably and repeatably reasoning about outcomes.

Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies.

Consequently, designing good verification loops is going to require a more holistic understanding of the systems under verification than simply the code. To have a verification loop that ensures sharding isn’t broken, you’d first need to understand how sharding is implemented, what a regression would look like, and how this can be identified using signals that can be quantitatively measured and compared.

These decisions become a pivotal part of the initial planning process before the coding agent even generates a single line of code. The coding agent will have to determine how critical pieces of data from the code that validate its correctness can be made available to external agents in the most ergonomic manner. Ideally, we want the strongest signals available to debugging agents from the topmost, shallowest layer (data that’s collected by default), rather than having to resort to Progressive Signal Discovery and descend many layers down the stack to find the signal most likely to lead to the right root-cause. In the case of the latency bug, had the application layer logged the number of DNS lookups it was doing, the strongest signal would’ve been available directly from Layer 1, without needing the agent to descend down to Layer 2 to procure this signal via DNS lookup details from a live production host.

Data Collection > Code Comprehension

While we’re on the topic of code, much of today’s agentic tooling features (better indexing, better retrieval, larger context windows, etc) are aimed at helping agents understand code. But code is an unreliable narrator, and in the case of both the “latency bug” and the “memory leak”, the agent’s first wrong answer came from reading the code.

The accurate root causes were derived from facts that an agent typically doesn’t check (DNS lookups on a production host, a heap profile, the kernel’s IPC tables). The software factory’s goal shouldn’t be to make code more readable for agents, but to help the agents gather better facts from the right layer at the right moment, and to do this enough times until the agent has what it needs to verify the right hypothesis.

Default Data Collection > On Demand Data Collection

Typically, the data needed for debugging is collected on an on-demand basis. This prolongs the debugging loop. Ideally, a software factory will have some mechanism to collect as much data as possible by default, so an agent has all the data it needs available to it right off the bat.

This requires the software factory to resort to techniques like having “always on” advanced data gathering from a small subset of production hosts, to perhaps even having a small subset of the production environment reserved purely for agentic experimentation.

Humans as Policy Setters > Humans as Meat Proxies

A large number of developers have devolved into being mindless meat proxies in the past year, where their sole contribution is blindly copying and pasting agent generated text around, or running specific commands on an agent’s behalf. This is the worst use of both the humans’ and the agents’ time. Humans are poor at processing large volumes of text, and agents flounder when having to work through a keyhole.

An agent-native factory’s goal should be to eliminate the use of a human as a meat proxy. Ideally, any human involvement should only be required when there’s some ambiguity involved in the final decision making process of the agent. Such events should further always act as an opportunity for evolving policies the agent can subsequently rely on.

Turn “Skill Issue” Into An “Infrastructure Issue”

Axioms such as “code doesn’t need to be read or understood anymore”, “loops solve everything”, “you just need more context engineering”, “just include more adversarial reviews” abound. Often, even the mildest scepticism of these supposedly self-evident truths get dismissed as a “skill issue”, where the “skill” in question is the ability to conjure rock-solid, bug-free, production-grade software merely by using a handful of “skills”, or prompting an agent effectively.

Conveniently, these dismissals rarely, if ever, go into precisely what the missing “skill issues” are, beyond mouthing the painfully insipid platitude of “just ask Claude to …”, where the “to” happens to be an ever-expanding list of software development practices, tips and tricks distilled into a few paragraphs of a markdown file.

In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to. It didn’t reproduce the “memory leak”, or constrain its hypotheses by the facts in the bug report, until I pointed it out. It didn’t back its claims in “the hang” with citations until I demanded them. Each time, what held the agent back wasn’t what it was capable of, but how far it was willing to go.

If an agent only debugs surgically and methodically when the person driving it knows how to get it to do so, then debugging really is a skill issue. The outcome of agentic debugging is then indeed a function of the individual skill of the developer performing the debugging, with the lessons learnt from each investigation staying confined to one person.

A more robust foundation can be built by investing in processes that allow an agent to go the whole hog by itself. The next great leap in agentic debugging is far more likely to come from better factories than relying on individuals to prompt better.

What Software Factories Are Missing

Almost all of the software factory implementations I’ve seen so far stress the importance of verification but gloss over the specifics of how the pre-production verification ought to happen. There’s also a lot of chatter about leveraging techniques like property based testing, formal methods of verification etc as a part of the agentic verification loop. What’s missing from these discussions is any mention of incorporating the kind of signals described in this post which are far more exacting at validating a change than just looking for passing tests.

In a book I published back in 2018, I’d proposed this testing quadriptych which details all of testing options available at each phase of the software development lifecycle. Agents are far better equipped than humans to conduct a suite of disparate tests at each of these phase, cross-referencing the data between tests, spotting regressions and anomalies, and more.

Develop Against Production

Once we have the infrastructure in place to allow agents to perform a panoply of such tests, we can shift testing left by bringing production closer to development. If you, like me, believe that all software development is going to happen via cloud agents, it’s imperative to ensure that agents can verify their changes as early as possible in the development lifecycle, and not wait until much later in the process to detect problems. This requires the development process to happen against an isolated slice of the production environment, with read only access to all signals, so a change can be tested against real production behavior as soon as it’s generated.

“Full Stack In A Box” Is Still An Anti-Pattern

One bad trend I’ve seen make a comeback is what I call the “full stack in a box” approach. About a decade ago, I wrote a post explaining why the “full stack in a box” approach for testing microservices was a bad idea. It’s an even worse idea to use this approach with agentic software development.

“Full stack in a box”, for those who’re not familiar with the term, is the approach where you run your entire production stack locally, including databases, caches, queues, etc, with agents monitoring or debugging some component of the “full stack”.

The main reason I believe “full stack in a box” is a bad approach for agents to use for debugging and verification is because the factual tier, which is the very linchpin of the agentic debugging loop described in this post, cannot be accurately replicated locally to match production. When your factual tier is unreliable or sparse, it’s very difficult for an agent to faithfully verify the change or zap through to the root cause.

It’s much more effective to ensure your debugging agent has the all the facts it requires directly from the production environment where the bug is observed, rather than spin up elaborate local test harnesses. Not to put too fine a point on it, but yes, this means figuring out how to give an agent access to your production environment so it can gather all the data it needs securely.

If it’s of any consolation, the security architecture underpinning this can be repurposed for many adjacent use cases, like running integration testing in production, so getting it right once is more than worth the while. Critically, this also enables development agents, and not just debugging ones, to tap into the same signals which allow for early regression detection.

Repurpose Debugging Framework For Integration Tests And Deploy Gating

The framework proposed in this post for debugging — picking a good control, identifying high-fidelity signals, with an adversarial reviewer involved in each stage — is something that would also work very well for integration tests, end-to-end tests, pre-deploy gates, automated canary analysis, and so forth.

With agents, the goal of testing isn’t just observing a binary final outcome (success vs failure), but checking for parity when it comes to every high-fidelity signal. Many of the signals used in past debugging incidents can also be baked into pre-deploy gating checks, to safeguard against regressions. In the case of the “latency bug”, if the pre-production testing environment had checked that the client’s DNS lookups matched those on the previous successful run, the routing bug would’ve been caught before it reached production, even at pre-production’s small scale.

Conclusion

The focal point of many public discussions around agentic coding happens to be the ultimate potential of these tools. The discourse seldom captures real world practicalities, or the realities of people building production software who have critical business needs and serve real users.

However, what I’m seeing happen in reality (and I’m willing to wager that mine is by far not an isolated experience) is that even as models become more capable, the engineers using them aren’t necessarily becoming vastly improved versions of themselves. In fact, agents can often amplify engineering weaknesses_,_ both individual as well as organizational.

Engineers who struggled with debugging complex problems continue to do so even with access to Claude Code, but often with far worse ramifications. While prior to using coding agents they may have sought help from a coworker when they failed to debug a problem, now I see them open PRs generated by Claude’s complete misdiagnosis of a problem. At best, such “non-fixes” fail to fix the problem. At worst, they introduce new bugs or break some other implicit functionality with a wide blast radius.

Codebases that accrue a plethora of such “non-fixes” become increasingly riddled with incongruence. A large number of “readability” complaints come from people manoeuvring such codebases that have degenerated into bloated artifacts of incoherence after being fed PR after PR of utterly empty calories.

Likewise, engineers who didn’t have much of an eye for detail aren’t suddenly producing code that’s well-structured, well-layered, mindful of performance and security implications, attentive to the impact on dependents (both direct and transitive), diligent about realistic edge-case handling, meticulous about telemetry soundness, etc. Sure, you can have a “skill” for all of this, but agents can take the “empty calories” approach, where each of these requirements are met cosmetically but not substantively.

The embrace of agentic paradigms for software development comes with trading understanding for speed. This doesn’t necessarily have to spell doom and gloom. It’s possible to ship high quality software at breakneck speed without sacrificing reliability, but it requires us to stop treating agents as oracles. Replacing a deep understanding of code with a deeper, higher-level understanding of systems, and a rigorous, regimented verification process like the one described in this post is the path forward.

This process, when applied consistently, can help build enough confidence in an agent’s ability to debug gnarly issues without requiring a human in the loop. While it calls for great focus, creativity, and assiduity to build such processes (and far be it from me to stake a claim to familiarity, let alone mastery in this area), the payoff is often a great reduction in time and effort required to debug any problem that might pop up in any layer of the stack you’d otherwise be too daunted to explore.

We now have the tools at our disposal that allow us to dream bigger and be inordinately more ambitious with our bets. This also requires a change in the epistemic discipline engineers use when working with agents. With a degree of creativity, and a sense of adventure, these ambitious bets are within easy reach, if we can only rise to the challenge.
